title: Omari
dek: A young voice preserving Babel’s stories while carefully distinguishing what the elders taught from what Omari has seen.

facts.Knowledge: Stories learned from parents and elders, distinguished from personal experience
facts.Last witnessed: Skylight Refuge · 5, Month of Moirah, Year 3

sources: Babel quest record · campfire testimony, August 2026
body:
Omari is a young survivor who carries Babel’s inherited stories into the conversations at Skylight Refuge. Those stories remember a garden, a Tree fed by human lives and a conquest that made the familiar world frightening. Omari also knows when to say that something has never been personally seen.

A young witness to life on the run

Omari joins the people listening to the adventurers and answers Olokun’s friendly questions about how they are recovering. Scars and apparent frailty first suggest age, but the account explicitly identifies Omari as young. The voice at the fire belongs to someone worn down early by flight.

The food of that flight is immediate testimony: worms and grubs eaten without cooking, because a fire’s light and smoke could reveal the group. Omari says that they are now healing. Gartina’s food and the chance to sit together allow a different kind of conversation from the work of staying unseen.

Stories and the limits of memory

Omari recounts what adults and elders taught about a floating island, the destruction of a great tree, and rulers who made both sunlight and darkness frightening. Omari explicitly says the floating island has not been personally seen. These stories preserve the community’s history without resolving every claim about the old catastrophe.

Moving between caves and jungles, the survivors try to map a landscape that seems almost alive. Stories keep the old walking and the young from growing weary. For Omari, memory is a practical resource for continuing, alongside shelter and food.

Physisia’s garden and the Tree of stories

Asked for a story, Omari describes a land once visited by the nature goddess Physisia and her lover Nami Iroh. Fruit trees sprang from her footsteps, and birdsong gave the measure of her voice. Nami Iroh spoke to the Tree throughout the day, feeding it the lives of the people who had loved, lived and died there. Their stories flowed downward with the water and nourished the ground.

In the tradition, the gods stopped returning for centuries. Omari does not claim to know why. Some people said it was their own sin, a blame Olokun tries to soften by assuring Omari that Physisia still fights for the world. His reassurance and the inherited explanation remain different voices; neither supplies a witnessed cause for the gods’ absence.

What the elders told about the conquest

Omari describes a ruler of the skies and a ruler of the depths, making both sunlight and darkness things to fear. In stories learned from elders, the Ice King drops the island in the sky to shatter the land and kill its Tree, then laughs as dust winter descends. The conqueror’s titles and creatures belong to that transmitted account.

When Olokun asks about the floating island, Omari is candid: adults tell of it, but Omari has not seen it. The adventurers bring their own sighting from beyond the mountains. Instead of pretending to be an eyewitness, Omari allows inherited history and new observation to meet. Kyrin’s memories preserve another, more personal account of the lost landscape.

Stories carried through a changing landscape

Olokun spreads out a map and asks where the survivors once lived. Omari answers with movement between jungle and caves, and attempts to map ground that seems almost like a living creature. When pressed, Omari again names the elder as the source. The words express how the community understands a difficult land; they do not establish that the entire island is literally a creature.

The purpose of remembering is less abstract. Stories keep the old walking and the young from growing weary. Omari carries them without claiming the rank of elder, ownership of planting knowledge or certainty about every event before birth. At a camp where a lost succession has made knowledge precarious, that careful telling preserves something the people can still pass on. Read Babel’s shared garden tradition →
